text: When David had finished speaking with Saul, Jonathan's soul was bound to the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul.
From that day on Saul kept David with him and would not let him return to his father's house.
Jonathan made a covenant with David, because he loved him as his own soul.
Jonathan took off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his armor, his sword, his bow, and his belt.

versions.text: Jonathan took off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his tunic, his sword, his bow, and his belt.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew מַדָּיו in a military context denotes a soldier's gear or armor rather than an undergarment. Since the following items are weapons and a belt, "armor" better conveys that Jonathan handed over his warrior's equipment.

text: David went out wherever Saul sent him, and he succeeded. So Saul put him in command of the fighting men, and this pleased all the people, and Saul's officers as well.

As they were coming home, when David returned from killing the Philistine, the women came out of all the towns of Israel to meet King Saul with singing and dancing, with tambourines and rejoicing and three-stringed instruments.

versions.text: As they were coming home, when David returned from killing the Philistine, the women came out of all the towns of Israel to meet King Saul with singing and dancing, with tambourines and joyful songs and lyres.
versions.explanation: בְּשִׂמְחָה means "with joy/rejoicing," not "joyful songs," which awkwardly duplicates the earlier "singing." Also שָׁלִשִׁים refers to a three-stringed (or triangular) instrument, not specifically lyres.

text: And the women sang to one another as they celebrated: "Saul has struck down his thousands, and David his tens of thousands."
Saul was furious; this saying displeased him deeply. "They have credited David with tens of thousands," he said, "but me with only thousands. What more can he have but the kingdom?"
And from that day on Saul kept a jealous eye on David.
The next day an evil spirit from God came powerfully upon Saul, and he raved inside the house while David was playing the lyre, as he did day after day. Saul had a spear in his hand,
and he hurled it, saying to himself, "I will pin David to the wall." But David eluded him twice.
Saul was afraid of David, because the LORD was with him but had departed from Saul.
So Saul sent him away from his presence and made him a commander over a thousand, and David led the troops out and brought them back.
In everything he did David had great success, for the LORD was with him.
When Saul saw how successful he was, he was afraid of him.
But all Israel and Judah loved David, because he led them out and brought them back.

Saul said to David, "Here is my older daughter Merab. I will give her to you as your wife; only serve me bravely and fight the LORD's battles." For Saul thought, "I will not lay a hand on him; let the hand of the Philistines be on him."
But David said to Saul, "Who am I, and what is my family, my father's clan in Israel, that I should become the king's son-in-law?"
So when the time came for Merab, Saul's daughter, to be given to David, she was given in marriage to Adriel of Meholah instead.
Now Saul's daughter Michal was in love with David, and when Saul was told of it, he was pleased.

"I will give her to him," Saul thought, "so that she may be a snare to him and the hand of the Philistines may be against him." So Saul said to David, "Now you have a second chance to become my son-in-law."
Then Saul ordered his servants, "Speak to David privately and say, 'Look, the king is pleased with you, and all his servants love you. Now become his son-in-law.'"
They repeated these words to David, but David said, "Do you think it is a small thing to become the king's son-in-law? I am a poor man, and little known."
When Saul's servants reported to him what David had said,

Saul replied, "Say this to David: 'The king wants no other bride-price than a hundred Philistine foreskins, to take revenge on the king's enemies.'" Saul's plan was to have David fall by the hands of the Philistines.

versions.text: Saul replied, "Say this to David: 'The king wants no other bride-price than a hundred Philistine foreskins, to take revenge on his enemies.'" Saul's plan was to have David fall by the hands of the Philistines.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew repeats "the king's enemies" in the third person; the pronoun "his" is ambiguous when read aloud (it could seem to refer to David), so retaining "the king's enemies" is clearer.

text: When the servants told David these things, he was pleased to become the king's son-in-law. Before the time had expired,

David went out with his men and killed two hundred Philistines. He brought their foreskins and counted them out in full before the king, so that he might become the king's son-in-law. Then Saul gave him his daughter Michal as his wife.
When Saul saw and knew that the LORD was with David, and that his daughter Michal loved him,
Saul feared David all the more, and he remained David's enemy the rest of his days.
Whenever the Philistine commanders came out to fight, David was more successful than all the rest of Saul's officers, and his name became highly honored.
